sounds.intro: Sumerian stopped being spoken around 1800 BC, so its sounds reach us through Akkadian scribes. Their sign lists spell out each sign's Sumerian reading in Akkadian syllables, their bilingual word lists give the meanings, and Akkadian borrowed hundreds of Sumerian words. All of it passed through Akkadian ears, which lacked some Sumerian sounds and may have missed others. What follows is the convention scholars share: close, but not a recording.

rows.note: A few scholars have argued for an o as well. Most do not accept it.

rows.ipa: b d g (or p t k)
rows.like: written b, d, g, but perhaps plain unaspirated p, t, k as in French
rows.note: Sumerian may have contrasted a puff of air (aspiration) rather than voicing. Akkadian heard the difference as voicing, which is why 'peg' appears as both gag and kak.

rows.ipa: p t k (or pʰ tʰ kʰ)
rows.like: like English p, t, k with a puff of air
probably trilled or flapped as in Spanish, not the English r
s as in 'sun'; z perhaps ts as in 'cats'
rows.note: Jagersma reconstructs z as the affricate ts. Many books simply read it as English z.

rows.like: ng as in 'sing', even at the start of a word
rows.note: Akkadian had no such sound, so its scribes wrote g, n, m or ng. That is why older books spell diĝir as dingir and -ĝu₁₀ as -mu.

rows.like: kh, the ch of Scottish 'loch' or German 'Bach'
rows.note: Some books leave off the mark and write h.

rows.like: unknown: something between d and r, perhaps an affricate like tsh
rows.note: Proposed because some words swing between d and r: du₃ 'build' is also read ru. When gud 'ox' takes a vowel it is written gud-ra₂ with the DU sign. Some scholars think no extra sound is needed.

rows.like: possibly a plain h or a catch in the throat between vowels
rows.note: Edzard and Jagersma argue for it from spelling patterns. The script has no sign that shows it.

rows.like: the same sound du; the small number says which sign was written
rows.note: Indices are modern bookkeeping from sign lists, roughly in order of frequency. Older books mark them with accents: dú for du₂, dù for du₃. ETCSL writes du₁₁ as dug₄.

rows.like: a reading whose sign has no agreed number yet
not read aloud: 𒀭 marks a god's name, 𒆠 a place
rows.note: Editions write them raised, like {d}en-lil₂ and unug{ki}. In this course you do not type them.

tips.p: Babylonian school lists such as Proto-Ea pair each sign with its reading spelled in small syllables, and bilingual lists add the Akkadian meaning. Loanwords help too: e₂-gal became Akkadian ekallum 'palace', and dub-sar became ṭupšarrum 'scribe'.
A sign can stand for a whole word or just a syllable, and often for several unrelated words. 𒀭 is an 'sky', diĝir 'god' and the silent god label. Context, and the endings around it, tell you which.
The main dialect, eme-gi₇, sits beside Emesal, used for goddesses' speech and temple laments. Emesal changes many sounds: 'my' is -ĝu₁₀ in eme-gi₇ but -mu in Emesal.

Nobody knows where Sumerian put its stress, whether it had tones, or how long its vowels were. The exact sounds of ĝ, ř and h are debated, and some common words have disputed readings: 7 is read imin or umun. Treat the pronunciation here as a shared convention.
